01 · The idea

One person, one move, everything written down.

Six guides, two towns, one man who lived the decision. His prices, the schools he walked into, the house he bought.

The brand is not the guides. The brand is the fact that somebody actually did this, and the guides are the proof.

The brand platform

Lived, not listed.

In one line: everything I learned moving my family to Madrid Norte, so you don't start from zero

What Patrick actually did · from the About page

  • ✓Researched the towns
  • ✓Searched the schools, himself
  • ✓Hunted the housing
  • ✓Bought a place off-plan
  • ✓Compared mortgages
  • ✓Lived through every piece of paperwork

That list is the asset. Everything else in this document protects it.

Nobody else shows their own move

Listing sitesEvery flat, today's price
Expat portals, forumsEverything about Spain
Relocation firmsA service, done for you
AI chatAn answer in ten seconds
Madrid UnpackedOne move, told straight“Our new-build house cost €605,000.” From the Colmenar Viejo guide.

The real rival is AI chat, outlined above. The About page says the aim is “to answer the questions when ChatGPT and Claude just don't cut it”. Keep that line: it names what the reader would use instead.

What this rules outDes · 23 Sep

Never publish what Patrick hasn't lived. The Tres Cantos schools guide already does this: three schools considered first-hand, the rest marked secondhand. That instinct is the brand.

It also means no Alcobendas, Pozuelo or Las Rozas just because people ask. The day the site covers a town nobody on it has lived in, it becomes one more expat portal.

One idea, and the four places it has to show up

The idea only counts if you can see it on the site. It shows up in four places, and each one gets its own section later on.

In the words

Section 09

The rule: say what we saw, and say what we didn't

Every school, price and street is marked one of two ways: first-hand, because we were there, or secondhand, because someone told us. The Tres Cantos schools guide already does it: three schools visited, two marked secondhand. Being open about what we didn't see is what makes people believe what we did.

In the name

Section 08

The rule: every guide title ends in “…, unpacked”

Tres Cantos, unpacked. Schools in Colmenar Viejo, unpacked. One title shape for every guide, so a reader knows what they're getting before they click. A topic Patrick hasn't lived doesn't get a title yet.

In the look

Section 10

The rule: black for facts, green for what we lived, handwriting for asides

The site looks like notes from a real move: typed facts, a green highlighter on the parts we lived through, and Patrick's handwriting for the things he'd say out loud. Nobody else can copy his handwriting.

In the business

Sections 07 · 13

The rule: the guides are free, the hour with Patrick is paid

The guides prove he knows what he's talking about. The only thing for sale is a €150 call with him, offered at the end of a guide, when the reader is thinking “but what about us?”

02 · The belief

The hardest questions about a move are the ones nobody will answer straight.

Patrick was shocked by how hard it was to find real answers. That shock is the founding story.

Which of the two towns?

The usual answerBoth are great for families.
From the guides“We were torn with Tres Cantos, but we just couldn't get excited about what the flats on offer there gave us for the same money.”Colmenar Viejo guide

Which school would you actually choose?

The usual answerHere are fourteen schools, in alphabetical order.
From the guides“I've focused this guide on the three schools we seriously considered ourselves.”Schools in Tres Cantos

Is the town centre as rough as it looks?

The usual answerA charming historic centre.
From the guides“The one area we wouldn't recommend is the town centre itself.”Colmenar Viejo guide

What does the extra money buy?

The usual answerPrices vary by area.
From the guides“A 3-bedroom flat in Tres Cantos will cost you more than — or about the same as — a new-build house with a garden in Colmenar Viejo.”Head-to-head

Usual answers: illustrations. Answers from the guides: quoted from Prototype 4.

A guide that won't say which school it wouldn't choose is a brochure. Honesty is the product, and the guides are how it ships.

The north star

The site a family finds in week one, and thanks in year one.

We don't measure success in visits. We measure it in one message: a family who moved here using the guides, writing back a year later to say the advice was right.

  1. Week oneThey find the siteEleven at night, fourteen tabs open, still deciding between the two towns.
  2. The months afterThey use it to decidePick a town, pick a school, maybe book the call with Patrick.
  3. Year oneThey write back“We went with your advice on the schools. You were right. Thank you.”
Why this, and not traffic

Traffic tells us people arrived. A thank-you a year later tells us the guide worked, in real life, for a real family.

It sells the call

That message is the most honest review there is. Put it next to the €150 offer and it does the selling.

It tests every new guide

Before publishing, one question: would this guide earn that message in a year? If not, it isn't ready.

Patrick can do it alone

No team, no ad budget, no growth tricks. Just guides good enough that people come back to say so.

How we'll know. A year after someone books a call, Patrick sends one question: “Looking back, did the guides get it right?” We count the yeses, and keep the best replies, with permission, for the site. Section 13 sets out the early numbers that tell us, month by month, whether we're on the way.

Specific over comprehensive · Lived over researched · Slow is fine

The discipline. Google is the channel; the parent is the reader. Write for the crawler and the reader can tell in one paragraph.

08 · The name

Madrid Unpacked. It was right the first time.

The working name has been the favourite since the first conversation, and the alternatives we tried only proved why. Every shorter, cleverer version lost either the city or the promise. This one keeps both, so the job here is not to replace it but to understand it well enough to build on it.

A name for a guide has one job: to be found and repeated by a parent who heard it once. Unpacked does that in both of its senses.

The story in the word

Nobody has questions on the day they arrive. They have them on the day they unpack.

Moving day is logistics. The real questions start a week later, standing in a kitchen full of boxes: which school, which side of town, was this the right pueblo, why is the paperwork like this. That moment, the first week after the van leaves, is when Patrick's family started collecting the answers that became these guides, and it is the moment the name points at. Unpacked means you have arrived and can breathe. Unpacked also means somebody took a subject apart and laid it out so you could see all of it. The site is the second kind of unpacking, written by someone who did the first kind a year ago.

Boxes unpacked · a subject unpacked · the same word, and the site is both

Why it holds

Keep

Does: the search, and the promise

“Madrid” is the word the parent types into Google at eleven at night, so it carries the traffic. “Unpacked” carries the tone: plain, a little domestic, not a firm. Together they are easy to say on a phone call, which is where most referrals to this site will happen, and easy to spell after hearing them once.

Two common words · one uncommon pairing · no explaining needed

What it gives the site for free

Device

Does: names every guide

The word is a verb, and that makes it a system. Every guide can carry it as its last word: Tres Cantos, unpacked. Schools in Colmenar Viejo, unpacked. Mortgages in Spain, unpacked. Each guide becomes one box opened, the site becomes the room, and a reader who has seen one title knows what every other one is. It also gives the seventh guide and the twentieth a name before they are written.

A naming device, not just a name · “…, unpacked”

The scope question, settled. The name says Madrid and the guides say two towns. That is a good problem. It gives the site a decade of room without ever renaming, and the hero line carries the honesty: Madrid Norte, for now. Do not fix it by adding “Norte” to the name, which makes it longer, harder to say, and wrong the day a third town arrives.

The collision to know about

unPacked Shop, Madrid's first plastic-free supermarket.

A zero-waste shop in the centre, written up by Time Out and the food-retail press, with an active Instagram at @unpackedshop. To a Madrileño, “unpacked” in Madrid already means groceries without plastic. It is a different sector, a different audience and a different trade-mark class, so it is not a reason to change the name. It is a reason to always write the two words together, never to shorten to “Unpacked” alone, and to check the Instagram handle before printing anything.

Not fatal · Never “Unpacked” on its own · Handle check before launch

09 · The language

Seven things the site says that nobody else can.

The prototype already has a voice, and a good one. This section writes down what it is doing so that guide seven sounds like guide one, and so that a machine answering questions from the guides is held to the same rules.

Owned words are what turn a blog into a place people quote, and they cost nothing.

ConceptWordWhy
The claim of experiencefirst-hand · secondhandEvery school, price and neighbourhood carries one of the two. The Tres Cantos schools guide already does this and it is the most trustworthy thing on the site.
The decision pagethe head-to-headAlready in use. It is the page the reader came for, so it gets a name and a fixed shape.
The verdict blockYou'll love it here if · It might frustrate you ifEvery guide ends with it, in the same words, in the same order. It becomes the thing people screenshot.
The real costwhat we paid€605,000, four bedrooms, 100m² of garden. A number with a date beats a range without one, and only somebody who paid it can publish it.
The productthe callLowercase, plain, and always described by what you bring to it rather than what it includes.
Every guide title…, unpacked“Tres Cantos, unpacked.” The name as a verb, so every guide is one box opened and the reader knows the shape before clicking.
When a fact goes stale or wrongupdated · we had this wrongPrices move and schools change heads. The fix is made in the text, dated, and the old line is left visible with a strike through it. A guide that shows its corrections is the only kind a reader trusts on the facts it hasn't corrected.

We say

Voice
  • First person, and “we” means the family. “We ended up in Colmenar Viejo.”
  • Numbers with dates. €500K to €650K, autumn 2026. Ranges age; dated ranges stay honest.
  • The con before the pro when the con is the thing people will hit first.
  • Which one. If asked which school, name the school, and say what it would depend on.
  • Spanish words for Spanish things: concertado, aerotermia, pueblo. Explained once, then used.

We don't say

Voice
  • “Relocation guidance”, “solutions”, “seamless”, “stress-free”. The firms' words, and they turn a person into a service.
  • “Hidden gem”, “vibrant”, “charming”. Listing-site words, and every one of them is a substitute for a fact.
  • “Expat” as a name for the reader. They are a family moving house.
  • Anything about a school, street or price that was not lived, without the secondhand badge on it.
  • Legal or tax advice. Patrick is a lawyer and is careful to say he is not one here. Keep that sentence.

The mortgages guide already does most of this. It says where the knowledge comes from (“comparing offers and securing our own”), explains each Spanish word once (tasación, arras, vinculaciones) and then uses it, and keeps the “I'm not a mortgage broker” line. Two things to add. A date on every rate and tax figure, because they change: “2.5–3.5%, autumn 2026”. And first-hand and secondhand marks, because the guide mixes what we did (comparing offers, getting our own mortgage) with rules we didn't live (non-resident lending, how UK and US mortgages work).

LineWhere it comes fromRead

Lived, not listed.Section 01Recommended as the brand line. Three words, it names the enemy without naming a company, and it survives under the wordmark, on a business card and at the end of an email.

10 · The look

A notebook, open on the kitchen table.

The site is one person's notes on one move, so it should look like them: warm paper, black ink, a highlighter, and the handwriting of the man who wrote it. The register comes from note-taking apps rather than from relocation, which all sits somewhere between an estate agent and a bank, and it gives the brand the one asset nobody can copy: Patrick's own hand.

Black ink for everything you read, a green highlighter for everything he lived, and his handwriting for the things he'd say out loud.

Paper#FBF6F1
Ink · every button#111111
Green · lived, Colmenar#C7EBB3
Peach · Tres Cantos#F4DFCD
Pink · the way forward#FFD5F8
White · every card#FFFFFF

The colour code. Green is Colmenar Viejo and anything Patrick lived, because it doubles as the highlighter: the €605,000 house, the school we visited, the neighbourhood we live in. Peach is Tres Cantos. Pink is only ever a way forward: the arrow circles and the call. Black is every button, white is every card. Nothing else gets a colour, so a reader learns the code in one page without being told it.

Contrast, said plainly. The three fills are pale on purpose, so they are only ever backgrounds, stickers and highlights. Text on them is always black #111, which passes comfortably on all three. Pale text on a pale fill is the one mistake this palette invites, and it is banned.

Type

Two typefaces and a strict split. Poppins does all the work: huge, bold and tightly tracked for headlines, regular for reading, semibold for every number. Shadows Into Light is Patrick's hand, and only Patrick's.

Headlines · Poppins 700

We ended up in Colmenar Viejo.

Big, bold, tight. The size carries the confidence so the words don't have to.

Reading · Poppins 400

The train is excellent, running the full length of Madrid from Chamartín down to Atocha. Parking in the old town can be a real pain.

Body, tables, captions, labels and every price, with tabular figures so columns line up.

Patrick's hand · Shadows Into Light

we'd do it again

Stuck-on notes only. A stand-in until Patrick writes a dozen of his own and they're scanned in.

The wordmark

Set in Poppins bold: “Madrid” in black ink and “Unpacked” on a stroke of green highlighter, exactly as it appears at the top of this page. It is the type and the colour code doing the logo's job, so there is no separate mark to design, protect or explain. A comma version, Madrid, Unpacked, is available for the wordmark alone, where it reads like a title and slows the eye in the right place. The domain, the handle and the spoken name stay without it.

The handwriting rule

The handwriting is the first-hand mark. It is also the easiest thing in the system to ruin, so it gets four rules of its own.

we paid €605K for ours9 min apart by train!good question!this is roughly us ↑
  • One to three notes per screen. More than that and it becomes a scrapbook.
  • Only things Patrick would say out loud. “We paid €605K for ours”, “good question!”. Never a label, a button or a heading.
  • Never the only place a fact lives. Every note repeats something in the typed text, so a reader who skips them, or a screen reader, misses nothing.
  • Black ink on a green, pink or white sticker, slightly rotated, never straight, never green on white.

Photography

Patrick's own photographs, taken on his phone, of the places the guides describe. No stock, no drone shots of the Sierra, nobody smiling at the camera; the children appear from behind or not at all. Framed in the same big rounded corners as the cards, with a handwritten sticker on the corner only where he'd actually have something to say. If a photo could be on a relocation firm's website, it is the wrong photo.

Two registers. The town register is the school gate, the platform, the park on a Tuesday, the building site in Tres Cantos North, photographed as they are. The lived register is the family's own life: the garden, the kitchen table with paperwork on it, the boxes. Only the lived photographs get a green “lived” tag and a handwritten note.

The shoot

Six photographs the site launches with, each with the brief it should be shot to. All six are a weekend with a phone. The images below are AI-generated placeholders to show the look; every one gets replaced by Patrick's own photo before launch.

Where the people are. Two of the six frames have the family in them, from behind. That ratio is right. The site is a person's notes, so a person has to be in it, but it is not a family blog, so the town gets more frames than the family.

What we never do

  • Stock photography of any kind. The first stock photo is the day the site stops being first-hand.
  • A map with pins and a compass. It says travel guide, and the site is not for visitors.
  • Suitcases, boxes, or a globe in the logo. “Unpacked” is a word, and it does not need illustrating. The mark is the wordmark.
  • Icons for the credibility strip. The audit said it and it holds: the three claims are stronger as three sentences.

Asset 01 · The fact card, one shape for both towns

Town guide · Autumn 2026

our real number, not a range

Colmenar Viejo

First-hand · we live here
Buy · 3-bed flat€320K–€450KGround floor, terrace, communal pool
Buy · 4-bed house€560K–€750KNew build with garden. We paid €605K
Rent · flat€1,000–€1,300Per month, 3 bed
Commute45 min trainC-4 to Chamartín · ~30 min by car
You'll love it here if
  • You want a garden and a house for the money
  • You're happy to speak Spanish every day
  • You want the Sierra half an hour one way, Madrid the other
It might frustrate you if
  • You want an English-speaking bubble
  • The commute matters more than anything
  • You'd rather move somewhere finished

The prototype's numbers, laid out as one component that both town guides share, with the price basis written under each figure instead of hidden in a hover. Prototype 4 moved that basis into a small (i) that only opens on hover. Phones have no hover, and most readers will be on a phone, so in practice nobody sees it. The badge at the top right is the first-hand mark from section 09, black with a green dot; on the Tres Cantos card it reads “First-hand · we nearly moved here”, which is true and is also the most honest thing a comparison site has ever said.

The verdict block travels. The two lists at the bottom are the end of every guide already. Putting them on the card means the head-to-head can show both towns' verdicts side by side without a single new sentence, and it is the shape people will screenshot to send to a partner.

One number to checkDes · 26 Sep

The prototype says the towns are nine minutes apart by train, and also that Chamartín is 28 minutes from Tres Cantos and 45 from Colmenar Viejo. On one line, those two claims give 17 minutes between the towns, not nine. One of the three figures is off, most likely the 45, which may include a wait or a walk. Could you check the C-4 timetable for a direct train and give me the three numbers as you'd put them on the site? The nine minutes is the most repeated fact on the site and the one I've drawn, so it is the one worth getting exactly right.

Where to invest. The fact card and the line are the two things a reader will connect to this site and nothing else. Every other visual decision, including how much of the current prototype survives, gets judged by whether it makes those two more recognisable.

What this document is doing. It is set in the register it proposes, so you are looking at the palette, the type and Patrick's handwriting on real content rather than on swatches. If it feels right here, it will feel right on a guide; if it feels like too much, the first thing to turn down is the number of handwritten notes.

11 · The screens

The whole site, page by page, in the notebook it will live in.

Section 10 on a page is a theory. This is the notebook applied to every page the site launches with, using the prototype's own copy where it exists and writing the missing pages where it doesn't. Press Focus on any window or phone to see it on its own.

Five pages, one grammar. If the reader can tell a guide from the about page by shape alone, the system is working.

The website, page by page

Home, the guides index, about, contact, and one full town guide. Three things changed from the prototype throughout: Patrick's handwriting sits on top of the typed page, the three fills do the wayfinding, and the call sits at the end of a guide rather than in the middle of the home page.

← Scroll sideways for the other pages · scroll inside a window to read it →

What the reference screens taught us here. The note-taking app you sent does three things worth copying: one huge black headline per screen, a round black button for every action, and stuck-on handwritten notes that make it feel like a person rather than a product. It does one thing not to copy: a little of its text sits pale on pale. Here, everything readable is black.

The app, as a sketch

Not release one, two or three. But the brand has a natural second surface: the ninety days after a family arrives, when the questions are small, daily and specific, and a website is the wrong shape for them. Nine screens, in the order a family would meet them, so we can see whether the idea holds all the way through or only on a home screen.

← Scroll sideways for the other screens →

Why the notebook, and not the two we tried first. Two other registers were explored on the way here, a warm photographic one and a soft pastel one, and both are kept in their own files. The notebook won because it is the only look this site can have and a competitor cannot: nobody else can put their own handwriting on a guide. It also happens to be the register the writing already speaks in, first person, honest, a little scrappy. It keeps one rule from each of the others: every photograph is Patrick's own, and pale colours are fills, never text. The risk it carries is the one it always had, handwriting used as decoration, and section 10 rations it for that reason.

Why this is here and not in the roadmap. An app costs a year and needs a reason to be opened every day. The website costs two months and needs a reason to be found once. Until the guides have a few hundred readers and a dozen calls behind them, the app is a sketch, and a useful one: it tells us the brand survives the move from a page to a product, that the colour code still works at phone size, and that the honest “not in the guides yet” state is the same idea on both surfaces. The last screen is the argument for building it eventually: it closes a loop the website can't.

12 · On one page

Madrid Unpacked, unpacked.

Everything above, in the shape the site uses for its towns. It is the card to keep open when a decision comes up that this document didn't foresee: a guide somebody offers to write, a sponsor who asks, a page that wants a new colour. If the answer can't be read off this card, the card is missing a line, and we add it here rather than deciding case by case.

One card, two lists. The brand is what holds when we say no to the second list.

Asset 03 · The brand, on its own fact card

Brand card · Autumn 2026

the whole thing, one card

Madrid Unpacked

First-hand · one move, told straight
The categoryFirst-hand relocation guidesNot a service, not a blog
The readerThe parent with fourteen tabs openDeciding in the next six months
The positionThe neighbour who moved in a year before youMadrid Norte, for now
The feelingBeing levelled withThe relief of a straight answer
The lineLived, not listed.Under the wordmark, at the end of every email
The device“…, unpacked”Every guide is one box opened
The codeInk · green · peach · pinkFacts · lived · Tres Cantos · the way forward
The productThe call · €150At the end of a guide, nowhere else
It holds if
  • Every school, price and street is badged first-hand or secondhand
  • Every number carries a date, and corrections stay visible
  • Green means lived, pink means go, and nothing else gets a colour
  • The handwriting says only what Patrick would say out loud
  • The call sits at the end of a guide, with a face and one sentence
It breaks if
  • A town gets a guide before somebody on the site has lived in it
  • A school, agent or developer pays to appear, even once
  • The copy starts to sound like a firm: seamless, stress-free, solutions
  • A stock photograph, a map with pins, or a suitcase in the logo
  • A guide is written for the crawler instead of the parent

The same component as Asset 01, with the brand in the place of a town. That is deliberate: if the brand fits its own fact card, the fact card is the right shape, and if a future decision can't be tested against the two lists at the bottom, it belongs on the list before it belongs on the site.

13 · Going to market

The guide is read once. The business is what happens at the end of it.

The go-to-market plan, in five parts: the situation we launch into, how one reader becomes a booking, where the first readers come from, what we do month by month, and how we measure it.

The situation we launch into

The readerOne parent, choosing between two townsOften moving from abroad or from Barcelona, with young children.
What we sellFree guides, one paid hourSix first-hand guides, and a €150 call with Patrick.
What we haveOne author, part-time, no ad budgetSo every channel has to be free and has to run on trust.
When they decideBefore MarchSchool applications in Madrid run in March (11–25 March in 2026). A family moving for September picks a town by about February.
The goal for the first six months live10 paid calls by the end of May 2027And a clear answer to where readers come from. A starting target: we revise it after the first month of data.

Launching at the end of November is good timing. It puts the site live just before the families it's for start deciding.

Where the first families come from

1

The main channel

Google

Slow to start, then it works on its own.

  • One question per guide, in the title
  • Its own web address for every guide
  • Search Console from day one, to see what people search
  • Future guides follow those searches, if we've lived them
2

The fastest start

Parent groups and forums

Where the fourteen tabs are open.

  • Expat and parent WhatsApp and Facebook groups, Reddit, Mumsnet
  • Answer the question properly first; link a guide only when it answers it
  • Patrick, under his own name
  • Half an hour, once a week
3

Slow, but trusted

People families meet first

School admissions teams, gestores, HR teams moving staff.

  • A short note and a one-page head-to-head they can pass on
  • No fees or commissions in either direction
  • Nobody is paid, or first-hand stops meaning anything

Not now: paid ads, influencers, a social posting schedule. We hold the handles and don't feed them yet.

Month by month, to the summer

  1. NovemberSoft launch5–10 families test the site. Fix what they find. Ask to quote them.
  2. Late Nov – DecLaunchGo live. Tell friends and colleagues. First answers in the groups. Analytics and Search Console on.
  3. January – MarchDecision seasonThe window that matters. Head-to-head and schools guides first on the home page. A dated note on the 2027 school application dates. Guide 7, the paperwork, published.
  4. April – JulyMoving seasonFewer people choosing, more people moving: the paperwork guide does the work. Ask callers for their stories. First full review of the numbers.

The 2027 application dates aren't announced yet; check the Comunidad de Madrid site in January. 2026 dates from comunidad.madrid.

What we measure

Four numbersThree from analytics, one we ask for.

01Where readers come fromGoogle, the groups, or a link someone sent.
02How many reach the verdictThe end of a guide is where the call sits.
03Call clicks and calls bookedPer guide, to see which one sells.
05Thank-yous a year laterAsked, not tracked. The number that decides if this works.

One blind spot. Links shared on WhatsApp usually show up in analytics as “direct” visits, so word of mouth is invisible there. We still ask everyone who books: how did you find us?

When Ask doesn't know, it says so and offers Patrick. That's the best lead the site gets: a real question the guides don't cover yet.

14 · The roadmap

Live in two months, then one guide at a time.

A tentative sequence, set to Patrick's rhythm rather than a deadline. The target is a live site around the end of November; if it becomes December, nothing is lost. The order matters more than the dates.

Release one is the prototype made real. Everything after it is one lived thing at a time.

What release 1 does not include. A Spanish version, a newsletter cadence, a seventh guide, or any town beyond the two. Each is a good idea and each one delays the launch, and the launch is what turns a prototype into a thing people can send each other.

What I need from youDes · 28 Sep

One thing from me, three from you, none of them long. The full list is in the roadmap above. Mine: the name is settled, so I buy madridunpacked.com and check the handles this week, before anyone else has the same idea. Yours: confirm the paperwork is guide seven. Take the six photographs on a weekend with your phone, or tell me which ones you'd rather not. And confirm the main contact button: Prototype 4 points it at email, while the proposal leads with WhatsApp because the audience is on a phone. That one choice sets how the call gets booked, so I'd like it to be a decision rather than a default.

With those done I can bring you the wordmark, the fact card designed rather than drawn, and the prototype restyled end to end so you can see the brand on the actual pages rather than in a document about them. Then we look at it together and decide what's right.

The role split as I understand it: you decide what goes in and how deep, I do the brand, the structure and the build, and we share drafts as links until there's a repo worth having. If that's off, one sentence back is enough.
